articles.headline: Treasury Designates Iranian Shadow Fleet Networks, Issues New General Licenses for Wind Down
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting five individuals, four entities, and nine vessels involved in Iran's 'shadow fleet' networks. These networks are accused of assisting in the transport and concealment of Iranian shipments, particularly oil, petrochemical products, and steel. Among the designated entities is a Panama- and Greek-based law firm, Karnakis and Karnakis, along with shipping businesses linked to Singapore and the United Arab Emirates.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis. Additionally, Iran General License HH was issued, authorizing wind down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026.

The action also included the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations. Furthermore, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, authorizing specific transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. Two amended Frequently Asked Questions, FAQ 1224 and FAQ 1225, were also released.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Middle East Eye / IranWire

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations, Issues Associated General Licenses to Combat Intellectual Property Theft
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are part of ongoing efforts to combat intellectual property theft.

Concurrent with these designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that might otherwise be prohibited. The specifics of the designated individuals or entities were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement.

This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to protecting American intellectual property and leveraging sanctions tools to deter and disrupt those involved in its theft. Further details on the scope of these designations and the accompanying general licenses are expected to be released.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License for Earthquake Relief, Updates FAQ
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 60A, titled "Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela." This amendment aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and recovery efforts in the country.

The original General License 60 was issued on June 25, 2026, and was set to expire on October 23, 2026. The amendment extends or clarifies the authorization for transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR part 591, specifically for earthquake relief.
In addition to the amended General License, OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further guidance and clarity regarding the authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates 27 Individuals and Entities Under Iran and Cuba Sanctions Programs, Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities under Executive Order 13902. These actions are part of Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" campaign, aimed at restricting Iranian financial and commercial networks.

Separately, OFAC designated Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank, under Cuba-related Executive Order 11404. In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses, including Iran-related General License FF, which authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

OFAC also issued a new Cuba-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1276) and an amended Russia-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 1225). The actions underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran's financial networks and Cuba's state-owned enterprises.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Official Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This action lifts sanctions on a prominent Venezuelan political figure, who has served as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly since 2021.

The removal covers five separate entries associated with Rodríguez, all sharing the same identifying information, confirming that the delisting concerns a single individual. This means Rodríguez is no longer subject to asset-blocking restrictions, allowing U.S. persons to engage in transactions with him that were previously prohibited.

While OFAC did not provide an explicit explanation for the decision, the removal is seen as a strategic shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela, potentially signaling a move from punitive economic containment towards structured access and engagement. This follows previous delistings of other Venezuelan officials and institutions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism sanctions programs. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorism financing networks.

The designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of these criminal organizations, preventing them from accessing the U.S. financial system and limiting their ability to conduct illicit activities globally.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the nature of their involvement in narcotics and terrorism, are expected to be provided in accompanying press releases from the Treasury Department.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates International Criminal Court, Issues General Licenses, and Announces Burma-related Designation Removal
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution under Executive Order 14203, which underpins the existing ICC sanctions regime. This action adds the entire ICC to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List.

Concurrent with the designation, OFAC issued four General Licenses (GLs) to authorize certain transactions involving the ICC. These include GL 13 for a 180-day wind-down period, GL 14 for telecommunications and enterprise software, GL 15 for pension payments, and GL 16 for transactions related to certain ICC detainees.

Additionally, OFAC announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics and a Burma-related designation removal. The designation of the ICC has been met with regret by the EU and condemnation from the UN Secretary-General, who warned of potential impacts on the court's work.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog / Al-Haq / Charity & Security Network / Shanraq.org

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Russia-related General License Authorizing Importation of Russian Diesel Fuel
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Russia-related General License 135, titled "Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin." This general license temporarily authorizes certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.

The issuance of GL 135 follows an announcement by the U.S. President regarding a deal with Russia to release 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to global markets, with additional amounts to follow. This action comes amidst rising diesel prices worldwide and appears to offer some relief for global energy markets.

However, the General License faces legal uncertainty, as it appears at odds with existing U.S. legislation targeting Russia's energy sector, including the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act. GL 135 does not authorize debits to accounts of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, the National Wealth Fund, or the Ministry of Finance.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Steptoe / Sanctions Alert

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Issues General Licenses for Iran and Amends Russia-related GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations as part of its ongoing efforts to counter illicit Iranian activities. These designations are likely to target individuals and entities involved in Iran's financial networks or support for its military and proxy groups.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Iran-related General License, the specifics of which were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement. This license is expected to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Iran sanctions program.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License. This amendment likely provides updated guidance or expands the scope of previously authorized transactions concerning Russia, reflecting ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 for 475 Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs. The violations targeted Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America processed payments involving blocked banks, failed to appropriately prioritize alerts for customers matching blocked persons, did not promptly update watchlists, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error. The total value of these apparent violations was approximately $14,834,082.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects no reduction to the base penalty, including no mitigation for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarding firm, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC's Illicit Drug Trafficking Sanctions Regulations and Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations. The settlement addresses four apparent violations of counter narcotics sanctions and six apparent violations of reporting obligations.

Between September 2023 and February 2024, Pegasus dealt in blocked property by facilitating the importation of a machine supplied by a designated company, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which had changed its name after designation. Pegasus also failed to respond fully for six months to an OFAC subpoena.

OFAC determined that Pegasus's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed. The settlement amount reflects consideration of general factors, including Pegasus's reckless disregard for sanctions requirements and its initial incomplete response to the subpoena.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $1,427,230 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. The specific details of the individual's identity and the nature of the violations were not immediately disclosed in the public record.

OFAC regularly imposes civil penalties on individuals and entities for breaches of U.S. sanctions laws, which can include engaging in prohibited transactions, dealing with blocked persons, or failing to comply with reporting requirements.
These enforcement actions serve to underscore the importance of adherence to OFAC regulations and the potential financial consequences for non-compliance, even for individuals.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC
body: Adani Enterprises Limited has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $275,000,000 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This substantial penalty highlights the serious consequences for companies, regardless of their global location, that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions.

The specific details of the violations leading to this significant fine were not immediately disclosed in the public record. However, such large penalties typically involve extensive and serious breaches of sanctions programs, potentially related to prohibited transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.

This enforcement action serves as a strong reminder to international corporations about the extraterritorial reach of U.S. sanctions laws and the critical need for robust compliance frameworks to prevent involvement in illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Signals Continued Vigilance on Inflation Amidst Mixed Economic Data
body: Federal Reserve officials indicated a continued hawkish stance on monetary policy, emphasizing that while inflation has shown signs of moderating, it remains above their long-term target. Recent economic data has presented a mixed picture, with some sectors showing resilience while others signal a slowdown. This has led to ongoing debate within the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) regarding the appropriate path for interest rates.

Analysts suggest that the Fed is closely monitoring core inflation metrics and labor market conditions, with any significant shifts potentially influencing future rate decisions. The central bank aims to strike a delicate balance, curbing inflation without triggering a severe economic downturn.

Market participants are keenly awaiting the next FOMC meeting for further clarity on the Fed's outlook and any potential forward guidance. The uncertainty surrounding inflation and economic growth continues to contribute to market volatility.

articles.headline: Global Oil Prices Fluctuate Amidst Geopolitical Tensions and Supply Concerns
body: Global oil prices experienced fluctuations this week, driven by a combination of ongoing geopolitical tensions in key producing regions and persistent concerns about supply disruptions. The recent U.S. decision to authorize certain imports of Russian diesel fuel, despite broader sanctions, has added a new layer of complexity to the energy market.

Analysts are closely watching developments in the Middle East, where regional instability continues to pose a risk to oil production and transit routes. Any escalation could lead to significant price spikes, impacting consumers and businesses worldwide.

The interplay between supply-side risks and demand forecasts, particularly from major economies, will likely dictate the trajectory of oil prices in the coming weeks. The market remains highly sensitive to news regarding production levels, inventory reports, and geopolitical events.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $350 Million Penalty on American Express National Bank for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced an enforcement action against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, imposing a $350 million civil money penalty. The penalty stems from significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program.

The OCC found that American Express National Bank failed to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs) and exhibited violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs. These deficiencies highlight systemic internal-control gaps and weak independent testing within the bank's BSA/AML framework.

This action underscores the OCC's continued focus on ensuring robust BSA/AML compliance programs within financial institutions. The penalty reinforces the accountability of banks and their management in preventing illicit financial activities.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Crowdfund Insider

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $750 Million Civil Money Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina. This penalty was imposed due to significant deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC found that Bank of America failed to timely file suspicious activity reports (SARs) and was responsible for sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. These failures contributed to the bank processing millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of various sanctions programs.

This enforcement action is part of a coordinated effort by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included penalties from FinCEN and OFAC, totaling over $1.21 billion against Bank of America for AML and sanctions violations. The OCC's penalty is the largest in its history.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / U.S. Treasury

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Order Against Former Vault Teller for Misconduct
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued an Order of Prohibition against Jennifer Hamblin, a former Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A. This action prohibits Ms. Hamblin from any participation in the affairs of a bank or other institution as defined in 12 USC 1818(e)(7).

Prohibition orders are utilized by the OCC against institution-affiliated parties (IAPs) to deter, encourage correction of, or prevent violations, unsafe or unsound practices, or breaches of fiduciary duty. These actions reinforce individual accountability for conduct related to a bank's affairs.
The specific details of Ms. Hamblin's misconduct leading to the prohibition order were not immediately disclosed in the OCC's general announcement of enforcement actions for October 2026.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
